lesson.title: When One Number Shouldn't Wreck the Whole Picture
lesson.summary: A resistant measure is a summary statistic that stays roughly stable even when a data set includes extreme values or outliers; the median and IQR are resistant, while the mean and standard deviation are not.
lesson.body:
A statistic is called resistant when its value barely changes if you move a small number of data points to extreme, unusual positions, or if you add or remove a single outlier altogether. This idea leans directly on two ideas you already have: the mean and the median as ways to describe the center of a distribution, and the concept of an outlier as a value that sits unusually far from the rest of the data. Resistance asks a practical question: if one strange data point showed up in your set, would your summary number still describe the typical case, or would it get dragged toward that one unusual point?

The mean and the median answer that question very differently, and the difference comes straight from how each one is built. The mean adds up every value in the data set and divides by how many values there are, so every observation, including an extreme one, contributes to the total. A single very large value inflates the sum, and therefore the mean, by an amount that grows the farther that value sits from the rest of the data. The median, on the other hand, is just the middle value once the data are sorted in order, or the average of the two middle values when there is an even number of observations. It only depends on which position a value occupies, not on how large or small that value actually is, so a value can be pushed arbitrarily far out and the median will not move at all as long as it stays on the same side of the middle.

Consider the annual salaries, in dollars, of seven employees at a small company: 42000, 45000, 47000, 48000, 50000, 52000, and 500000 for the founder. The mean of all seven salaries is 784000 divided by 7, which is 112000 dollars, a number that does not describe a single one of the six ordinary employees. The median, the fourth value once the list is sorted, is 48000 dollars, right in the middle of where most employees actually fall. Now remove the founder's salary and look at the remaining six employees. The new mean is 284000 divided by 6, about 47333 dollars, a drop of nearly 65000 dollars from before. The new median, the average of the third and fourth sorted values, 47000 and 48000, is 47500 dollars, a shift of only 500 dollars. One extreme value swung the mean by tens of thousands of dollars while barely nudging the median.

This is exactly what resistance means in practice, and it is why statisticians reach for the median, along with the interquartile range, whenever a distribution is strongly skewed or contains outliers, such as incomes, home prices, or reaction times with a few very slow trials. The mean and the standard deviation remain extremely useful tools, especially for roughly symmetric data without extreme values, but they should not be trusted blindly whenever a data set has a long tail or a handful of unusual observations.

Recognizing resistance also tells you how to read a summary you did not compute yourself. If a report gives you a mean income for a neighborhood, ask whether a few very high earners could be inflating that number; if it gives you a median, you can trust it to reflect a more typical household. This same logic will resurface constantly, from comparing the mean and median to detect skew, to deciding whether the range or the standard deviation better describes spread, so it is worth internalizing now rather than memorizing later.
